Yes — let’s decode that .eep (Intel HEX / EEPROM) file to make it human-readable and understand its structure.

Your file contents:

:0F00000048656C6C6F2C20776F726C64210A005E
:00000001FF
🔍 Step-by-step breakdown

Intel HEX format uses lines that look like this:

:llaaaatt[dd...dd]cc
Field	Meaning
:	Start code
ll	Byte count — number of data bytes
aaaa	Address (16-bit) — where data should go
tt	Record type (00 = data, 01 = EOF, etc.)
dd...	Data bytes (in hex)
cc	Checksum
🧩 Decode your first line
:0F00000048656C6C6F2C20776F726C64210A005E

Breakdown:

Field	Value	Meaning
:0F	0x0F = 15 bytes of data	
0000	Address = 0x0000	
00	Record type = data record	
Data	48 65 6C 6C 6F 2C 20 77 6F 72 6C 64 21 0A 00	actual bytes
5E	checksum	
🧠 Convert data bytes to ASCII
Hex	ASCII	Description
48	H	
65	e	
6C	l	
6C	l	
6F	o	
2C	,	
20	(space)	
77	w	
6F	o	
72	r	
6C	l	
64	d	
21	!	
0A	\n (newline)	
00	null terminator	

So, the data string is:

"Hello, world!\n"
✅ Second line
:00000001FF

Breakdown:

Field	Value	Meaning
:00	0 bytes of data	
0000	address 0x0000	
01	EOF record	
FF	checksum	

→ End of file marker.

🧾 Summary — Human-Readable Representation
Address	Data (Hex)	ASCII
0x0000	48	H
0x0001	65	e
0x0002	6C	l
0x0003	6C	l
0x0004	6F	o
0x0005	2C	,
0x0006	20	(space)
0x0007	77	w
0x0008	6F	o
0x0009	72	r
0x000A	6C	l
0x000B	64	d
0x000C	21	!
0x000D	0A	\n
0x000E	00	null terminator
🧠 Conceptually

So, this .eep file encodes the EEPROM contents for:

char e2str[] EEMEM = "Hello, world!\n";

It starts at EEPROM address 0x0000, stores the ASCII text "Hello, world!\n", followed by a null byte (\0) — exactly how a C string is represented.

Would you like me to show how to convert arbitrary .eep files to readable text automatically (e.g. with a small Python script)?

Sun, Oct 26 at 11:37 PM
Sure, make a script

Here’s a clean Python script that decodes an .eep (Intel HEX) file and prints its contents in a human-readable format — both as ASCII text and structured data.

🧩 decode_eep.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
decode_eep.py — Convert an .eep (Intel HEX) file into a human-readable view.
Usage:
    python decode_eep.py your_file.eep
"""

import sys
import binascii

def parse_hex_line(line):
    """Parse a single Intel HEX line into (address, record_type, data_bytes)."""
    if not line.startswith(":"):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line: {line}")
    line = line.strip()
    byte_count = int(line[1:3], 16)
    address = int(line[3:7], 16)
    record_type = int(line[7:9], 16)
    data = bytes.fromhex(line[9:9 + byte_count * 2])
    return address, record_type, data

def decode_eep(filename):
    memory = {}
    with open(filename, "r") as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.strip() == "":
                continue
            address, record_type, data = parse_hex_line(line)
            if record_type == 0x00:  # data record
                for i, b in enumerate(data):
                    memory[address + i] = b
            elif record_type == 0x01:  # EOF
                break
    return memory

def dump_memory(memory):
    # Print table
    print("Address | Hex  | ASCII")
    print("----------------------")
    for addr in sorted(memory):
        b = memory[addr]
        ch = chr(b) if 32 <= b <= 126 or b in (10, 13) else "."
        print(f"0x{addr:04X}  | {b:02X}  | {ch}")
    # Print ASCII view
    print("\nASCII dump:")
    data = bytes(memory[addr] for addr in sorted(memory))
    try:
        text = data.decode("ascii")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        text = data.decode("latin1")
    print(repr(text))

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python decode_eep.py <file.eep>")
        sys.exit(1)

    filename = sys.argv[1]
    memory = decode_eep(filename)
    dump_memory(memory)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
🧠 Example Run

If your file (example.eep) contains:

:0F00000048656C6C6F2C20776F726C64210A005E
:00000001FF

Then running:

python decode_eep.py example.eep

prints:

Address | Hex  | ASCII
----------------------
0x0000  | 48  | H
0x0001  | 65  | e
0x0002  | 6C  | l
0x0003  | 6C  | l
0x0004  | 6F  | o
0x0005  | 2C  | ,
0x0006  | 20  |  
0x0007  | 77  | w
0x0008  | 6F  | o
0x0009  | 72  | r
0x000A  | 6C  | l
0x000B  | 64  | d
0x000C  | 21  | !
0x000D  | 0A  | .
0x000E  | 00  | .

ASCII dump:
'Hello, world!\n\x00'

Perfect — yes! You can absolutely extend the .eep decoder to automatically generate an Arduino-style .ino file that embeds the EEPROM data as a byte array and writes it to EEPROM in setup().

Here’s a complete version that does exactly that 👇

🧩 eep_to_ino.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
eep_to_ino.py — Convert an .eep (Intel HEX) file into an Arduino .ino sketch
that writes the EEPROM data back into the chip.

Usage:
    python eep_to_ino.py input.eep output.ino
"""

import sys

def parse_hex_line(line):
    """Parse a single Intel HEX line into (address, record_type, data_bytes)."""
    if not line.startswith(":"):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line: {line}")
    line = line.strip()
    byte_count = int(line[1:3], 16)
    address = int(line[3:7], 16)
    record_type = int(line[7:9], 16)
    data = bytes.fromhex(line[9:9 + byte_count * 2])
    return address, record_type, data

def decode_eep(filename):
    """Return EEPROM bytes as a dict {address: byte}."""
    memory = {}
    with open(filename, "r") as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.strip() == "":
                continue
            address, record_type, data = parse_hex_line(line)
            if record_type == 0x00:  # data record
                for i, b in enumerate(data):
                    memory[address + i] = b
            elif record_type == 0x01:  # EOF
                break
    return memory

def generate_ino(memory, output_file):
    """Create an Arduino sketch that writes the EEPROM bytes."""
    sorted_addrs = sorted(memory)
    data_bytes = [memory[a] for a in sorted_addrs]
    byte_list = ", ".join(f"0x{b:02X}" for b in data_bytes)

    ino_content = f"""#include <EEPROM.h>

// Auto-generated from EEPROM image
byte data[] = {{{byte_list}}};
const int data_len = sizeof(data);

void setup() {{
    Serial.begin(9600);
    Serial.println("Writing EEPROM contents...");
    for (int i = 0; i < data_len; i++) {{
        EEPROM.write(i, data[i]);
    }}
    Serial.println("EEPROM write complete!");
}}

void loop() {{
    // Nothing here — EEPROM written in setup()
}}
"""
    with open(output_file, "w") as f:
        f.write(ino_content)
    print(f"✅ Arduino sketch written to {output_file} ({len(data_bytes)} bytes).")

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python eep_to_ino.py input.eep output.ino")
        sys.exit(1)

    input_eep = sys.argv[1]
    output_ino = sys.argv[2]

    memory = decode_eep(input_eep)
    generate_ino(memory, output_ino)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
🧠 Example

If your file example.eep is:

:0F00000048656C6C6F2C20776F726C64210A005E
:00000001FF

Run:

python eep_to_ino.py example.eep eeprom_loader.ino

Output file eeprom_loader.ino will contain:

#include <EEPROM.h>

// Auto-generated from EEPROM image
byte data[] = {0x48, 0x65, 0x6C, 0x6C, 0x6F, 0x2C, 0x20, 0x77,
               0x6F, 0x72, 0x6C, 0x64, 0x21, 0x0A, 0x00};
const int data_len = sizeof(data);

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(9600);
    Serial.println("Writing EEPROM contents...");
    for (int i = 0; i < data_len; i++) {
        EEPROM.write(i, data[i]);
    }
    Serial.println("EEPROM write complete!");
}

void loop() {
    // Nothing here — EEPROM written in setup()
}
🔧 Notes
This uses EEPROM.write() from <EEPROM.h>, standard on AVR-based Arduinos.
It writes the bytes sequentially starting at address 0x00.
You can upload the generated .ino sketch to your Arduino, and it will restore the EEPROM content automatically.

Would you like me to modify this so it only writes bytes that differ from the current EEPROM contents (to preserve EEPROM lifespan)?
